title: ‘Lanterns’ Trailer: Hal Jordan Visits Sinestro in Prison, Guy Gardner Has a Cameo and a Shape-Shifting Manhunter Is on the Loose
description: HBO’s upcoming DC Studios drama “Lanterns” got a new trailer for the Green Lantern-inspired mystery at San Diego Comic Con. The eight-episode series
body:
HBO’s upcoming DC Studios drama “Lanterns” got a new trailer for the Green Lantern-inspired mystery at San Diego Comic Con. The eight-episode series premieres on HBO on Aug. 16.

	The show stars Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan, a veteran Green Lantern, and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, Jordan’s protege who is learning the ropes. The heroes have magical rings that allow them to create any object imaginable out of green light. They patrol the galaxy and keep peace as members of the Green Lantern Corps. In “Lanterns,” the two outer space cops get called into rural Nebraska for a mysterious murder, which may have connections to dangerous extraterrestrials.
	

	The cast includes Kelly Macdonald, Laura Linney, Paula Patton, Garret Dillahunt, Poorna Jagannathan, Nicole Ari Parker, Jason Ritter, Sherman Augustus, Paul Ben-Victor and Ulrich Thomsen as the classic Green Lantern villain Sinestro. Nathan Fillion, who played Green Lantern member Guy Gardner in last year’s “Superman” and its upcoming sequel “Man of Tomorrow,” will be back in “Lanterns.”


	The new trailer revealed the first look at Sinestro, who has a complicated past with Jordan. In the comics, Sinestro was a former Green Lantern and mentor figure to Jordan, but the red-skinned alien flips and becomes one of Jordan’s greatest villains. He later becomes a Yellow Lantern, an opposing space group who uses fear to power their magical rings. There’s also a cameo from Guy Gardner, plus it’s revealed that the murder mystery surrounds the Manhunters, a race of aliens who can shape-shift and look like anyone.

	“Lanterns” is created by Tom King, Damon Lindelof and showrunner Chris Mundy. They also serve as executive producers alongside DC Studios co-CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran. “Lanterns” joins “Creature Commandos” and “Peacemaker” as fellow shows in the rebooted DC Universe. Up next for the DCU is this fall’s body-horror movie “Clayface,” starring Tom Rhys Harries as the classic Batman villain.
	

	Watch the trailer below.

body:
Hasbro is launching a brand new “My Little Pony” series exclusively on YouTube. 

	Titled “My Little Pony: Forever Frienship,” the show will debut on YouTube in early 2027. Nine-minute episodes will drop bi-weekly. The series is said to follow “Twilight Sparkle, Pinkie Pie, Rainbow Dash, and Fluttershy as they embark on a new journey of friendship, magic and self-discovery.” 

	The cast includes Jenna Weir as Twilight Sparkle, Ava Preston as Rainbow Dash, Kayla Samson as Fluttershy and Kaya Kanashiro as Pinkie Pie. Gretchen Mallorie serves as showrunner and head writer, with Tayhan Mustafa as series director. The series was developed in collaboration with Lil Critter Workshop and features artistic contributions from illustrator Nicholas Kole. 
	

	“For over forty years, ‘My Little Pony’ has remained one of Hasbro’s most beloved and enduring franchises, connecting with generations of fans around the world through stories rooted in friendship, imagination and creativity,” said Kim Boyd, president of global licensing & entertainment for Hasbro. “With ‘My Little Pony: Forever Friendship,’ we’re continuing to grow the brand through fresh storytelling, a visionary creative team and new entertainment experiences designed to inspire today’s audiences while staying true to the heart of what fans have always loved about ‘My Little Pony.’”


	Hasbro has also unveiled the new music track “Forever Friendship” from vocalist Cali Rodi and produced by Super Weirdo Productions.

title: Noah Wyle on ‘The Pitt’ Fan Discourse, Saving Hollywood and What’s Coming In Season 3
description: Noah Wyle knows some “The Pitt” fans came down hard on his character, Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, given how the character’s personal struggles
body:
Noah Wyle knows some “The Pitt” fans came down hard on his character, Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, given how the character’s personal struggles caused him to lash out at some of his colleagues in Season 2. But he tries not to pay attention to the online discourse.

	“The blending of the line between actor and part that I sometimes see, where an actor is blamed for the behavior of a character, or where a character’s dialog stops being representative of the character and starts being representative of the creative team — as if they’re saying something that they believe through this particular vehicle — I think gotten a little blurry as viewers have sort of conflated character message and character,” he tells Variety‘s Awards Circuit Podcast. “It doesn’t necessarily have an encoded message because somebody’s saying it. Other than the dramatic tension within that one scene, it’s not necessarily trying to be representative of anything larger.”
	

	Wyle says he believes it’s still just a small but very vocal portion of the viewership that is piling on — but he prefers not to be engaged with the more negative conversations that might be out there. “My skin is is too thin to really engage anything that might be coming at me, so I tend to want to say live and let live, and I’ll go do my job, and you can take what you want from me.”


	Wyle does say that his son would sometimes warn him when the backlash against Dr. Robby got very heated online: “My son is the one who calls me and goes, ‘Dad, they’re really mad at you.’ He’s my firewall. He’ll go, ‘Dad, you might not want to go to the market today unless you start treating Dr. Mohan better!”
	

	Wyle understands that the vitriol that came at Dr. Robby this year “was disappointment that he was acting less heroic than he presented himself last year. But when we’re at our most desperate, we’re not always our most graceful. And we were trying to show somebody who was going through a mental health crisis and was behaving irresponsibly, unprofessionally and out of character for himself as he was asking people to see him in his moment of plight and potentially stop him from doing himself harm. That did get misinterpreted by some people as him just being misogynistic or cruel. I think there was a much bigger picture at play.”

	On this edition of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, “The Pitt” star, executive producer and director Noah Wyle — Emmy-nominated three times this year — discusses the wild fan reaction to Season 2 and Dr. Robby’s storyline, as well as how “The Pitt” is showing how to keep production jobs in Los Angeles. But first, the Roundtable looks at the TV Academy’s decision to move five categories out of the Emmy telecast and the debate over whether this will make a difference in producing a more entertaining ceremony. Listen below!

	Wyle has been a big advocate of bringing production back to Los Angeles, and “The Pitt” — shot locally here on the Warner Bros. lot — has put him front and center in the conversation. “I’m looking at it from the standpoint of somebody who has grown up in and around this industry and befriended people who are generations deep in this industry who’ve watched it really crater over the last couple years,” he says. “There is still an abundance of talent here, and ‘The Pitt’ is is proof of what you could do with that talent when you when you apply it. That, I feel, is being grossly overlooked in the pursuit of tax credits or to circumvent union protections, as work not only leaves the state but leaves the country.

	“I think ‘The Pitt’ economically has proven that it’s still cost-effective to shoot in Los Angeles if you keep your footprint small and you make certain considerations at the outset that in the event of a success, a rising tide lifts all boats,” he adds.  “When we started shooting the pit on the Warner Bros. lot, it was a bit of a ghost town. The only thing that was happening there were the tours going through empty sound stages, talking about the work that used to be done there. And now it’s a fairly buzzy place, so I’m hoping that there’s a trend.”
	

	Despite some of the rougher discourse we mentioned above, Wyle says he’s pleased that most of the reaction about Dr. Robby’s mental health journey in Season 2 has been positive. “We hoped that once you got past the architecture of the protagonist having a nervous breakdown in a mass casualty event, the aggregate toll of an average shift in the average life of an average career would be compelling enough television,” he says. 

	“And Season 2 was a bit more speculative than one because of that, and more gratifying to see the response, because it reaffirms that there’s a narrative here that doesn’t necessarily need to revolve around a stunt, like an air show disaster or something massive to really keep viewers’ attention.

	“It’s incredibly gratifying to be on a show that has resonance and is being spoken about at all,” he adds. “It’s also really gratifying to be involved in a show that’s saying something that sparks conversation and of an intimate nature. You want to be a water cooler show. You want things that people have differing opinions on, so that those ideas and debates can happen in the marketplace, and people can arrive at consensus and hopefully find commonality in that process. I think a lot more bridges have been built through this show than have been burned.”

	As for next season, the show is moving to November — a chilly month that will provide a bit of contrast to what we’ve seen so far. “We wanted to play with a different season,” Wyle says. “We just came off of hot July 4, so it seemed appropriate to plot it a little into a different season. We wanted Robby to have been away from the hospital for a little while, and so both of those things felt like fall would be appropriate. Everybody’s turning on their heaters again. The first rains caused slick roadways, different kind of cases, different asthetic.”




	

	



	Wyle’s first appearance in Variety was on Feb. 9, 1990, for the NBC miniseries “Blind Faith.”

	“Given my level of participation in that event, my grandfather watched both segments and said, ‘I had to watch an awful lot of Blind Faith for a little bit of Noah,'” Wyle recalls. “The real story is that somebody had told me that you had to say seven words to get a SAG card, and my line was five words long. It was ‘What’s going on down there?!’ I spent all morning trying to figure out how to stretch it to seven. And when the director said action, I said ‘Excuse me, what’s going on down there?!’ And then I found out it didn’t matter. I didn’t have to say seven words.”


	10 QUESTIONS WITH NOAH WYLE:
	

	1. Childhood nickname: “‘Wile E Coyote,’ from ‘Road Runner,’ I got called Wile E. Coyote a lot growing up, or ‘Noah’s Ark,’ obviously.”

	2. Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into it now: “Oh my goodness, I’m still into everything I was into as a kid. But I had an unnatural obsession with ‘Grease 2.’ I know every word to ‘Grease 2,’ and sometimes alone in my car, will do renditions of ‘Cool Rider.’ I’ve befriended Chris McDonald, who played Goose, he was the tall T-Bird, and I’m sure he’s so annoyed with how many times I bring that movie up.”

	3. Go-to Karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song: “It’s a massive phobia that I’ve been grappling with for most of my life. I got shamed young and scared to sing publicly, so it’s been one of my great desires to be able to have confidence. Even the mention of the word ‘karaoke’ makes me break out and sweat. Because it usually means I’m being forced to do something I’m not comfortable with. But I’m working on it. I usually warm up slow with something that Rex Harrison could handle.” [What about alone in the shower?] “That’s when I go full ‘Dreamgirls’ cast album.”

	4. Give me an alternate title for your show:  [Not asked]

	5. What’s your secret talent?: “Acting. Don’t tell anybody. It’s my only talent.”

	6. Favorite ice cream flavor: “I like McConnell’s mint chip ice cream a lot, but I also like peanut butter and chocolate ice cream from Haagen Dazs. That was when I got in my youth a lot. And I was part of the ’70s sherbert craze.”

	7. The one item you couldn’t live without: “My wife. I’m not calling my wife an item. I’m just saying that I really, really depend heavily upon her.”

	8. What TV show in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of?: “‘Deadwood,’ without hesitation. I’ve always wanted to do a western, and I loved that show. David Milch’s writing was poetry punctuated with profanity, and I would have given anything to have been in the room with Ian McShane and Tim Olyphant and Keith Carradine and some of the actors on that show. I just loved it. We had Brad Dourif, who played the doctor on ‘Deadwood.’ He’s the father of Fiona Dourif, who plays Dr. McKay. I got to tell him how much I enjoyed his performance, which I thought was so flawless. That man could put more intention into a syllable than anybody I know.”

	9. Fictional character you most admire: “I most admire Atticus Finch, probably. It’s infused with Gregory Peck’s performance. I saw it at a formative age, and there’s that moment at the end when up at the balcony, Jim and Scout are told to stand. ‘Stand up, Jim, your father’s passing.’ And the quiet dignity and heroism of Atticus always loomed large for me.”

	10. Your favorite piece of advice: “The first one that comes to mind is George Clooney early on saying, ‘Take your work seriously. Don’t take yourself seriously.’ That was a big one. I remember I saw an interview once with former Boston Celtic great Bill Russell — and I don’t like giving any credit to anything Boston Celtic, but Bill Russell is not your average Boston Celtic — and he said that he learned later in life that it was far better to understand than it is to be understood. And that we spend so much time trying to get our own personal points of view across, and so little time trying to listen to everybody else’s, that we sometimes do ourselves a disservice. So I latched onto that one too.”
	

	Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more. Subscribe via Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or anywhere you download podcasts.

title: ‘Interview With the Vampire’ Renewed for Season 4, Titled ‘Queen of the Damned’
description: “Anne Rice’s Interview With the Vampire” has been renewed for Season 4, titled “Queen of the Damned.” The renewal was announced at San Diego Comic C
body:
“Anne Rice’s Interview With the Vampire” has been renewed for Season 4, titled “Queen of the Damned.” The renewal was announced at San Diego Comic Con and comes ahead of the Season 3 finale on Sunday for “The Vampire Lestat.” 

	Series executive producers Mark Johnson and Hannah Moscovitch and stars Jacob Anderson, Assad Zaman, Eric Bogosian and Sheila Atim were on stage at Comic Con to discuss “The Vampire Lestat” and announced the renewal. The new season is based on Rice’s third novel, “Queen of the Damned.” Moscovitch will serve as showrunner and executive produce along with Johnson and Rolin Jones.
	

	“In ‘The Vampire Lestat,’ Mark, Rolin, Hannah and this extraordinary cast delivered an unforgettable season filled with propulsive storytelling that captivated the passionate and engaged fans of this franchise,” said Dan McDermott, Chief Content Officer of AMC Global Media and President of AMC Studios, in a statement announcing the renewal. “We can’t wait to continue the journey with ‘Queen of the Damned,’ one of the most iconic stories in Anne Rice’s mythology, and watch our established and beloved characters confront Akasha with their world, and ours, very much hanging in the balance.”


	“The Vampire Lestat” is technically the third season of the “Interview With the Vampire” series, but was rebranded to signify it would be adapting Rice’s second novel of the same name. Aspiring rock star Lestat (Sam Reid) is the focus of the third season, in which he gives journalist Daniel Molloy an interview for his film. Among his vulnerable confessions include a detailed recollection of his first love, Nicolas de Lenfent (Joseph Potter), who became a vampire with Lestat.
	

	“Interview With a Vampire” first premiered in 2022, marking the second adaptation of Rice’s 1976 novel. The Tom-Cruise-led film was the first to bring the story to life in 1994.

	To accompany Lestat’s journey to become a rock star, the series produced 20 songs sung by Reid, including “Your Biggest Fan,” “All Fall Down” and a cover of Billy Idol’s “Dancing With Myself.”

title: Chuck Russell, Director of ‘The Mask,’ Dies at 74
description: Chuck Russell, who helped launch several notable careers as the director of genre films including 1994’s “The Mask” as well as “A Nightmare on Elm S
body:
Chuck Russell, who helped launch several notable careers as the director of genre films including 1994’s “The Mask” as well as “A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors,” died Wednesday in the San Diego area. He was 74. 

	His death was confirmed by his attorney. The local fire department had responded to his house for the report of an unconscious man, according to TMZ.

	Russell started out writing screenplays and working as a production manager and assistant director on independent films. He met Frank Darabont while working as an executive producer on “Hell Night,” and went on to collaborate with him. 
	

	He wrote the script for Dennis Quaid-starrer “Dreamscape,” directed by Joseph Ruben. Russell then made his directing debut on “A Nightmare on Elm Street 3,” which helped revitalize the franchise and grossed more than the first two installments as well as launching Patricia Arquette’s career. He went on to helm the cult favorite remake of “The Blob.” 

	For 1994’s blockbuster “The Mask,” he cast Cameron Diaz in her first movie and made Jim Carrey a household name. The film earned an Oscar nomination for visual effects. 

	Russell’s next films were “Eraser,” with Arnold Schwarzenegger, and “The Scorpion King,” the first leading role for Dwayne Johnson. 

	After several years of hiatus, Russell returned to direct “I Am Wrath” with John Travolta, the Indian action-adventure film “Junglee” and “Paradise City” with Bruce Willis and Travolta.

	In 2024, he directed a remake of “Witchboard,” and told Variety at the time, “We have to humanize these things, whether it’s action or comedy or drama,” he says. “You gotta get into your performers’ heads. You gotta get their actual personality into their performances.”
	

	He recently announced two productions with his AI company Neumorphic, “Hyperia” and “b,” which the company said were “built with generative AI across their entire production pipeline.”

schema.headline: Chuck Russell, Director of ‘The Mask,’ Dies at 74

title: Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial
description: Paramount Skydance has reached an agreement with a coalition of state attorneys general to postpone the Warner Bros. Discovery merger until after an
body:
Paramount Skydance has reached an agreement with a coalition of state attorneys general to postpone the Warner Bros. Discovery merger until after an antitrust trial.

	The company entered a joint stipulation in the federal case on Friday afternoon agreeing not to close the $111 billion transaction until five days after a trial is held or June 1, 2027, whichever is earlier. No trial date has been set, but the agreement likely puts the merger on hold for at least several months.
	

	A coalition of 12 states, led by California, obtained a temporary restraining order earlier this week that blocks the merger from closing for 28 days, pending the outcome of motion for a preliminary injunction. The states allege that the deal will reduce competition in the cable and theatrical markets, and should be blocked.


	“Halting this merger while our case proceeds is a critical victory in our efforts to uphold the law and protect the film and television industries,” said New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, in a statement. “I look forward to continuing our case to stop this illegal merger.”

	California Attorney General Rob Bonta, meanwhile, declared the agreement a “tremendous win.”

	“Our argument against this illegal merger is straightforward: When too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse,” he said. “Today’s agreement is great news for audiences, movie theaters, and the many people who write, build, and create the art, news, and entertainment so many of us enjoy. We are eager to continue to make our case in court and celebrate another tremendous win in our effort to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day.”
	

	Norm Eisen, co-founder of the Democracy Defenders Fund and a member of the #BlocktheMerger campaign, also hailed the agreement as a victory for grassroots opposition to the deal.

	“The Ellisons believed their relationship with President Trump would help them push through a disastrous deal that threatened democracy, creative freedom, and independent journalism. We in the #BlocktheMerger campaign helped prove them wrong,” he said. “This collective resistance is turning the tide.”

	Paramount had been keen to close the deal before Sept. 30, when it will begin to incur a $7-million-a-day “ticking fee” to be paid to Warner Bros. investors. The agreement is a tacit acknowledgement that that will not happen, barring a settlement with the states.

	Paramount previously sought a three-day hearing on the injunction motion in late August, hoping to win the judge’s blessing to close the deal sometime in early September. 

	But the states resisted that idea, saying they would need more time to take discovery and prepare for a full trial on the merits. The states were due to file their injunction motion on Thursday night, but held off as the two sides held discussions on a path forward.

	In a statement, the company said the agreement is a “significant win.”

	“Today’s agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence,” a Paramount spokesperson said. “This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers, and good for creators, a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached. Plaintiffs’ market definitions bear no relationship to the realities of today’s marketplace and cannot withstand scrutiny. We look forward to proving our case at trial.”

	A hearing was scheduled for Aug. 3 in federal court in Oakland, at which point the two sides were expected to argue over the injunction motion. The two sides agreed to cancel that hearing.

	U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin approved the joint stipulation on Friday afternoon, about an hour after it was entered.

	The Writers Guild of America filed its own motion for an injunction earlier this week, which was also set to be heard on Aug. 3. That motion has been withdrawn, as Paramount has effectively conceded that it will not close the deal until a determination of the merits of the antitrust claims.
	

	The parties also agreed to submit a joint stipulation by July 31 on their respective positions on trial scheduling. The states previously proposed to hold the trial in April 2027.

schema.headline: Paramount Agrees to Postpone Warner Bros. Merger Until After Antitrust Trial

title: Warner Bros. Discovery Sues Amazon, Accusing It of ‘Lawless Employee Shopping Spree’ Including Poaching HBO Veteran Pia Barlow
description: Warner Bros. Discovery sued Amazon, alleging the internet giant engaged in an “illegal” campaign of “inducing contracted employees” of WBD to “breac
body:
Warner Bros. Discovery sued Amazon, alleging the internet giant engaged in an “illegal” campaign of “inducing contracted employees” of WBD to “breach their employment agreements” — including HBO marketing veteran Pia Barlow.

	In its lawsuit, WBD alleged that “Amazon has chosen to ride on the coattails of other well-established Hollywood mainstays such as Plaintiffs” by poaching their employees “rather than build its entertainment-production workforce from the ground up.”
	

	Warner Bros. Discovery said “there is perhaps no better example of Amazon’s lawless employee shopping spree” than its hiring of Barlow, formerly senior VP of originals marketing at HBO Max. Amazon MGM Studios announced Friday that it had hired Barlow in the newly created role as head of original series marketing. Barlow is slated to start at Amazon on Aug. 3, reporting to global head of marketing Sue Kroll.


	According to WBD’s lawsuit, Barlow’s employment contract was not set to expire until Oct. 31, 2027. Barlow “freely and expressly committed to remain employed” with WarnerMedia Services “for the duration of the term,” the lawsuit said. “Though it was aware of Barlow’s ongoing contractual commitment to WMS, of which WBD is a beneficiary, Amazon has brazenly and deliberately induced Barlow to breach the employment agreement by packing up and decamping to Amazon more than 16 months before its expiration.”

	When Amazon offered a higher pay package to Barlow, she “promptly discarded those commitments, demonstrating that her contractual promises were worth honoring only until a richer offer appeared,” the Warner Bros. Discovery suit said. “Amazon recognized that Barlow’s loyalty was for sale.”
	

	Amazon MGM Studios declined to comment on Warner Bros. Discovery’s lawsuit.

	WBD filed the suit on July 21 in California Superior Court for the County of Los Angeles, Central District. “Amazon must be stopped; it should not be permitted to profit from its illegal and tortious behavior,” Warner Bros. Discovery said in the suit. The complaint seeks unspecified monetary damages and “injunctive relief as a result of Amazon’s willful and malicious interference in Plaintiffs’ contractual relationship with Barlow.”

	“In blatant disregard of established California law, Amazon has gone rogue by attempting to induce Plaintiffs’ employees with term employment agreements to breach those agreements with impunity, backed up with the ready assurance that Amazon will defend and indemnify them should they be held to account for their blatantly unlawful acts,” WBD’s lawsuit said.

	According to the WBD lawsuit, Barlow informed the company of her intention to terminate her employment “prematurely” on May 26, 2026, and submitted her formal resignation notice on June 5. “Barlow’s actions conveyed a troublesome message throughout Plaintiffs’ executive ranks that contractual commitments may be disregarded, including whenever a larger paycheck appears, undermining the stability that term employment agreements are specifically intended to provide,” Warner Bros. Discovery alleged. 

	Moreover, Amazon “did not merely promise Barlow legal representation; it selected for her one of its own, hand-picked outside law firms” that has a long-standing relationship with Amazon and is based less than a mile away from Amazon’s primary global headquarters in Seattle, per the WBD lawsuit.

	Barlow “is not the first (nor, apparently, the last) WBD employee that Amazon has targeted or will target in the future,” according to the lawsuit. According to Warner Bros. Discovery, just a few weeks before Amazon’s “interference with Barlow’s term employment contract,” Amazon “similarly endeavored to tortiously induce another WBD employee to breach their term employment agreement,” which was not set to expire until December 2027. “Fortunately, in that instance, Amazon ultimately was unsuccessful in its efforts to raid WBD’s workforce as to that particular executive,” according to the WBD complaint.
	

	Warner Bros. Discovery’s lawsuit claimed that “Amazon is currently in the process of attempting to interfere with the term employment contract of at least one other WBD executive.”

	In the suit, WBD accuses Amazon of intentional interference with contractual relations; inducing breach of contract; intentional interference with prospective economic advantage; and unfair competition in violation of California law.

title: Emmys 2026 Voters’ Guide: Breaking Down the Early Frontrunners
description: While down-the-line voting has often scored huge, the 2026 Emmys may shake up the usual tradition. Some of the biggest shows of the year are only r
body:
While down-the-line voting has often scored huge, the 2026 Emmys may shake up the usual tradition. Some of the biggest shows of the year are only recognized in the acting categories but miss in series nods. Below, Variety breaks down the contenders in a few major categories. (And here’s a full list of the nominations, in case it helps!)

	Drama

	In the drama category, last year’s winner, “The Pitt,” which also took home lead actor, supporting actress and guest actress trophies, is back with its second season. It leads the pack in overall nominations with 25 — 13 of which are for actors. This time, “The Pitt” faces two other HBO Max series in the category: “The Gilded Age” and “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms.” Netflix’s “The Diplomat” and Hulu’s “Paradise” landed series nods, one of the seven total noms for each show. Apple TV also scored three noms in the category; “Slow Horses” earned its third nomination in the category while new series “Pluribus” and “Your Friends & Neighbors” both broke into the race. While “Pluribus” garnered a whopping 18 nominations for its first season (and Rhea Seehorn is the front-runner for lead actress), the recognition in this category is the sole nom for “Your Friends & Neighbors.” Meanwhile, Brad Ingelsby’s “Task” didn’t earn a series nod, but did get recognition for writing, directing, cinematography and editing, as well as acting noms for Mark Ruffalo (lead actor) and Tom Pelphrey (supporting).
	

	 Guest actor/actress, drama

	Last year, “The Pitt” racked up 13 nominations; this year, that’s the number of actors from the show that received their kudos, with five in the guest actor and guest actress categories. Ernest Harden Jr., Jeff Kober, Brittany Allen, Tal Anderson and Tina Ivlev all landed recognition for the medical drama, despite some not even being submitted by HBO; instead, they self-submitted. But will they cancel each other out? It’s always a possibility with multiple nods in one show. The guest actor category includes other heavy hitters too: Colman Domingo for the final season of “Euphoria,” Jeff Hiller for “Pluribus,” Bradley Whitford for “The Diplomat” and Jonathan Pryce for “Slow Horses.” On the guest actress side is early front-runner Shailene Woodley for “Paradise,” Miriam Shor for “Pluribus” and Merritt Wever for “The Gilded Age.” 
	

	 Comedy series

	With “Hacks” breaking the record for most-nominated comedy series (24), and it being the final season of the beloved HBO Max comedy, it seems like an easy front-runner. That being said, it’s not an easy category, with mostly returning shows filling the category — FX’s “The Bear,” ABC’s “Abbott Elementary,” Netflix’s “Nobody Wants This,” Hulu’s “Only Murders in the Building” and Apple TV’s “Shrinking.” But the two new series in the batch are serious contenders: Apple TV’s “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” which racked up eight nods, and, even more so, the spoiler of the race, Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay.” The horror-comedy scored 19 nominations, including six acting noms — Matthew Rhys earned lead actor noms for both this and limited series “The Beast in Me” — and nods for writing, directing and casting.

	 Guest actor/actress, comedy

	Some of the biggest stars landed in the guest actor and actress in a comedy categories this year. Two-time Emmy winner Rob Reiner earned a posthumous nomination for his role in “The Bear,” one that will be hard to beat. But if anyone could do it, it’d likely be the beloved Michael J. Fox, who landed a nomination for “Shrinking.” Elsewhere in the stacked category is Christopher McDonald for “Hacks,” Hamish Linklater for “Widow’s Bay,” Brett Goldstein for “Shrinking” and “Heated Rivalry” star Connor Storrie for his hosting role on “Saturday Night Live.” For guest actress, Jamie Lee Curtis (“The Bear”) and Betty Gilpin (“Widow’s Bay”) are the only two not from “Hacks,” as Cherry Jones, Laurie Metcalf, Leslie Bibb, Lauren Weedman and Kaitlin Olson account for the remainder of the group. Once again, canceling out could happen, but the odds are good that “Hacks” could do very well on Emmy night.



	

									Disney
	



	 Limited or anthology series

	For its first season, Netflix’s “Beef” won the trophy for best limited/anthology series. This time around, the show hasn’t generated quite as much buzz, but it still earned 16 nominations, including for lead actor and actress and supporting actor and actress. Elsewhere in the category is Netflix’s “The Beast in Me,” FX’s “Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. & Carolyn Bessette,” Peacock’s “All Her Fault” and HBO Max’s “DTF St. Louis.” The latter also landed a slew of acting noms with Linda Cardellini, Joy Sunday, Jason Bateman, David Harbour and Richard Jenkins filling up the supporting categories. Although “All Her Fault” was an early drop, released in November, star Sarah Snook took home a Critics’ Choice trophy and the show snagged two Golden Globe nominations and an Actor nod. Although “Monster: The Ed Gein Story” came up short in the series nomination, star Charlie Hunnam still snagged a lead actor nom, and Laurie Metcalf earned her second nom of the year for her supporting role in the Netflix horror drama. Netflix’s “Death by Lightning” and Prime Video’s “Bait” failed to land series noms, but the actors were recognized; Nick Offerman landed a supporting nod (his second of the year alongside a supporting comedy actor nod for “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”) and Riz Ahmed earned a limited lead actor nomination.
	

	 Reality

	As we seem to write over and over again, one of the most difficult categories to break into has always been reality competition, with years of the same winners. At one point, “The Amazing Race” won in seven consecutive years, then “RuPaul’s Drag Race” won four years in a row. For the last two years, “The Traitors” has taken the trophy. This year, “The Amazing Race” is out of the running and ABC’s “Dancing With the Stars” is back for the first time in 10 years, which shouldn’t come as much of a surprise after its massive 34th season. “Top Chef” and “Survivor,” which also had a huge season with its 50th, round out the category with four of the five nominees also recognized in host: RuPaul, Jeff Probst, Kristen Kish and Alan Cumming. Ariana Madix was the surprise fifth spot for her hosting of Peacock’s “Love Island USA.” Who becomes a front-runner may come down to who campaigns best during phase two.

The Coalition of Asian Pacifics in Entertainment and Janet Yang Productions have granted four filmmakers $25,000 to produce their films as part of the Julia S. Gouw Short Film Challenge.

	The filmmakers include Keshni Kashyap Nilsson (“The Shoe Burglars”), Nayon Cho (“Stigma”), Patricia Lee (“Wasted Resources”) and Tiffany Lin (“Hunger”). The Short Film Challenge’s jury is comprised of “Moana” star Auli‘i Cravalho, “Anora” producer Samantha Quan, “Take Me Home” director Liz Sargent, “Bridgerton” actor Yerin Ha and “Stop! That! Train!” executive producer Chris Quintos Cathcart.
	

	“After five years of our program continuing to grow, we have substantial evidence that it is achieving everything we had hoped for,” Short Film Challenge founder and Emmy award-winning producer Janet Yang said in a statement. “New filmmakers are being discovered and supported in the most beautiful way — at top festivals, with key players in the industry. Equally important, they have been given a chance to realize their full creative voice, bringing dream projects to fruition.”


	The initiative supported Sargent’s short back in 2022 that eventually became her 2026 feature, “Take Me Home,” which won Sundance’s top screenwriting honor earlier this year. 

	“In a landscape where representation continues to rise and fall, successes from the API women and non-binary filmmakers coming out of this Short Film Challenge demonstrate the importance of continuing to uplift these stories despite decreased gender and racial diversity in Hollywood,” CAPE‘s head of programs Rhian Moore said in a statement.
	

	This is the fifth year of the challenge. The short film program will end in a celebratory screening showcase in November.

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

									HBO Max
	




	Primetime Emmys Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: July 24, 2026): With the Television Academy officially revealing this year’s Emmy nominees, attention turns not only to who’s in the running but to which episodes the actors are submitting. Though the Emmys have increasingly become dominated by buzz and momentum, official episode submissions can still play a critical role. But as full-season sweeps have become more common, it’s worth asking: Does the individual episode carry the weight it once did?

	That question will occupy strategists and pundits over the next few weeks. Only a handful of categories have published their selections, which you can find on each category page.

	Supporting comedy actress offers the early intrigue, with two sets of double-dippers: Hannah Einbinder and Megan Stalter of the HBO Max comedy “Hacks,” and Dale Dickey and Kate O’Flynn of the Apple TV comedy “Widow’s Bay.” Dickey and O’Flynn chose the same episode, “Beach Games,” which is inarguably a showcase for O’Flynn. With the May 31 cutoff, Dickey was unable to submit what many would have assumed was the no-brainer, “Emergency Shelter,” in which Rosemary delivers a hilarious slide presentation tracing the lineage of the curse plaguing the town.

	Einbinder, like lead actress co-star Jean Smart, selected the series finale. Stalter went with “QuikScribbl,” the episode that strips Kayla of her Porsche, her trust fund and her office space. Supporting comedy actor nominee Paul W. Downs submitted the same half-hour.

	Lead comedy actress has its full slate up for viewing. Smart’s “Hacks (Finale)” is the closing statement of a four-time winner. Quinta Brunson opted for “Night Out” from the ABC mockumentary “Abbott Elementary,” Ayo Edebiri chose “Worms” from FX’s “The Bear,” and Elle Fanning submitted “Lock and Load” from the Apple TV freshman comedy “Margo’s Got Money Troubles.” Lisa Kudrow, back in the fold for the HBO Max comedy “The Comeback,” went with “Valerie Faces Reality,” an ideal showcase for a performance that could spoil Smart’s night.

	Supporting drama actor is a more revealing exercise, in part because “The Pitt” landed three nominees and all three chose differently. Patrick Ball submitted “8:00 P.M.,” when Langdon gets his confidence back. Shawn Hatosy took the season finale, “9:00 P.M.” Gerran Howell went with “7:00 P.M.,” in which Whitaker gives a pep talk to Ogilvie in the ambulance. The staggered approach keeps the trio from cannibalizing one another on the same hour of the shift, but with a cast this sprawling, will it work?

	Tom Pelphrey, a possible front-runner for the HBO Max drama “Task,” is submitting “Vagrants,” the episode where Robbie takes Tom hostage. Elsewhere, two-time Emmy winner Billy Crudup, the sole nominee for the penultimate season of Apple TV’s “The Morning Show,” chose “The Parent Trap.” Also from Apple TV, Jack Lowden went with “Circus” from “Slow Horses,” while Carlos-Manuel Vesga selected “The Gap” from “Pluribus.”

	Only two of the top series nominees have chosen their six episodes for consideration: HBO Max’s “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” and Apple TV’s “Slow Horses.”
